headline: Both Majors are fixed and their guards have teeth (12 of 12 B07 breakage checks killed; all 19 of run 1’s probes pass). Five Minors remain in the area, one of them new with the fix: switching Capture back on can bring a false push before the shell syncs again.

findings.title: Capture switched back on (or access granted again) after a day: a false “Capture may be off” push the next morning, until the shell syncs again
findings.detail: The fix counts the 24 hours from the listener’s own last connected heartbeat. But the shell sends no heartbeat when the listener connects: `CaptureListener.onListenerConnected` only logs locally, and `CaptureSwitch.apply(true)` rebinds after the batch’s heartbeat (saying the listener is off) has gone. So the server keeps reading “off since <days ago>” until the next sync (a payment, opening the app, or the daily work), and the morning job can push meanwhile. Inside the shell, Home can show the server’s “listener off since …” banner while the phone itself says it’s connected. In run 1 any heartbeat counted, so this is new with the fix. Server side run; the shell’s side read in the code, not run (no device). One fix: enqueue a sync from `onListenerConnected`.
findings.repro: pnpm exec vitest run --config qa/B07/vitest.probe.config.ts qa/B07/api-probes-run2.probe.ts -t "Capture switched back on"
findings.evidence:
switched on 1 h ago, no connected heartbeat since: silent no-heartbeat; next-morning pushes 1; body «Sen hasn’t heard from your phone for a day. Open Sen to check it can still read notifications.»
AssertionError: expected [ { …(2) } ] to have a length of +0 but got 1

findings.title: The listener-off push says “Sen hasn’t heard from your phone for a day” although the phone synced an hour ago
findings.detail: `captureWatchdog` picks its words by `silent`; `no-heartbeat` now also means “the listener has been off for a day while syncs arrive”, and the push still says the phone went quiet. Home words the same state as “Sen’s listener on your phone has been off since …”. One fact, two wordings, which the eyes pass asked to end.
findings.evidence:
listener off: at 23 h pushes 0; at 25 h pushes 1, silent no-heartbeat, listenerConnected false, lastListenAt 2026-11-02T23:08:23.741Z; push body «Sen hasn’t heard from your phone for a day. Open Sen to check it can still read notifications.»
AssertionError: expected 'Sen hasn’t heard from your phone for …' not to match /hasn.t heard from your phone/

findings.title: Paging still loses events whose posted time has sub-millisecond precision
findings.detail: `/sync` accepts and stores microsecond instants, but the cursor carries `toISOString()`, milliseconds only, so rows between the cursor’s millisecond and the last row’s microsecond fall between pages. The shell sends milliseconds, so only a hand-made client reaches it. Truncating `posted_at` to milliseconds on insert, or a microsecond cursor, would close it.
findings.evidence:
microsecond postedAt accepted: 200 synced 51 refused []
sub-ms: stored like 02:00:00.000150, 02:00:00.000149; pages 2; distinct seen 50 of 51
AssertionError: expected 50 to be 51

findings.title: A phone clock days behind fakes “No payment notifications for 2 days” while payments arrive daily
findings.detail: An event now counts at `least(posted_at, created_at)`, which trusts a phone clock that is behind. D143 (7) says the watchdog counts from the server’s clock; `created_at` alone would (an offline phone is caught by the heartbeat rule anyway). Run 1’s `max(posted_at)` had the same flaw, so it isn’t new; finding 4 fixed the clock-ahead half only.
findings.evidence:
phone 3 days behind, a payment every day: lastEventAt 2026-10-31T22:08:23.982Z, silent no-events; pushes 1
AssertionError: expected [ { …(2) } ] to have a length of +0 but got 1
